title: Guido Keller — the Eagle of Fiume: Milan to the Roadside
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Milan — the birth of the von Kellerer heir
stops.campa: On 6 February 1892 Guido Keller is born in Milan, into an aristocratic family of Swiss and German descent — the von Kellerer. The city is the industrious capital of the North, but the child is made for none of its ledgers. From the first he is ungovernable: a boy who will be expelled from the Swiss college of Trotzen for want of discipline, who reads Graf and dreams the East. The Lombard fog does not hold him. He is already, though no one yet knows it, the wildest spirit the coming pirate-republic will produce.
suggested_refs: Portraits of the young Guido Keller in aviator's dress

stops.name: Fiesole — the family's Tuscan hill
stops.campa: The Kellers settle at Fiesole, on the olive terrace above Florence, and the Milanese aristocrat becomes half-Tuscan. Under the tutelage of the poet Arturo Graf in Turin the young Guido takes his education, but it is the light of the hills and the classical air that shape him. Here the seed of the yogi-anarchist is planted: he begins already to read the Vedanta, to distrust the settled life, to want a discipline that is not the college's but the spirit's. Florence Florentinises him; the eagle is not yet on his shoulder, but it is coming.
suggested_refs: Fiesole, the Etruscan hill above Florence

segments.name: L'asso da caccia — the fighter ace, 1915–1918

stops.name: Cameri — the pilot's brevet
stops.campa: At the Cameri field near Novara, Keller earns his pilot's brevet in December 1914. The machines are frail lattices of wire and canvas, and he takes to them as to a natural element — the man who will one day sleep in a tree already prefers the air to the ground. On 1 December 1915 he receives his commission in the Corpo Aeronautico Militare. The war has begun; the aristocrat who cannot obey a schoolmaster will obey the sky, and the sky rewards him.
suggested_refs: Aviatik B.I and Nieuport-Macchi trainers of the Corpo Aeronautico Militare

stops.name: Verona-Tombetta — the Carso combats
stops.campa: Flying from Verona-Tombetta and the fields of the Isonzo front, Keller wins his spurs over the Carso. In February 1917 he challenges an Austro-Hungarian pilot to weaponless single combat — the victor to be whoever seizes the other's tail. Keller wins the chivalric duel, and the astonished enemy escort him courteously back across the line. Three times over these years he will be decorated with the Silver Medal for Military Valour, proposed even for the Gold. The ace is a knight of an older war.
suggested_refs: Silver Medal for Military Valour (three awards)

stops.name: The 91ª Squadriglia — under Baracca, the squadron of aces
stops.campa: On 1 November 1917 Keller is posted to the 91ª Squadriglia — the legendary squadron of aces under Francesco Baracca, Italy's greatest airman. He downs at least three enemy machines, confirmed, and helps bring down many more. When Baracca falls over the Montello in June 1918, Keller flies alone over the enemy line to seek him, and bears the great ace to his grave among the pallbearers. The prancing black horse of Baracca's fuselage becomes the emblem of a whole age of aviator-poets.

stops.name: Godega di Sant'Urbano — shot down, captured, freed at Vittorio Veneto
stops.campa: In the last days of the war, strafing low near Godega di Sant'Urbano, Keller's machine takes enemy fire and he is badly wounded in the legs. He is captured and lies hospitalised behind the Austrian line — until the Italian breakthrough at Vittorio Veneto in late October 1918 liberates him. The war ends with victory, and with the word that will curdle the whole generation: mutilata, the mutilated victory. Fiume, promised and withheld, becomes the wound around which men like Keller will organise their lives.

segments.name: La Santa Entrata — the march on Fiume, September 1919

stops.name: Ronchi — the night muster with the Comandante
stops.campa: At Ronchi, in the night of 11–12 September 1919, Keller is among the officers gathered about Gabriele d'Annunzio for the mad and holy enterprise. The grenadiers are won over; Major Reina consents; the trucks are found. Keller, the wounded ace who cannot bear the peace, is at the Comandante's side from the first hour — he will be the only legionary permitted to address the poet with the intimate tu. At dawn the column sets out for the city on the Quarnaro, and the pirate-republic of poets is born on the road.

stops.name: Fiume — the Santa Entrata, the Holy Entry
stops.campa: On 12 September 1919 d'Annunzio's column enters Fiume to delirious welcome — the Santa Entrata. The Comandante is fevered but erect; the city that Versailles denied to Italy is taken by a thousand irregulars and a poet. Keller rides in with them, into the wildest political dream of the century: a city-state of legionaries, arditi, futurists, deserters, dreamers. Here, on the Adriatic edge, the aristocrat-ace becomes something without precedent — a yogi-anarchist in uniform, and soon the Comandante's chosen hand for every impossible deed.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the legionaries of the Santa Entrata, Fiume, September 1919

stops.name: Fiume — Segretario d'Azione and the Ufficio Colpi di Mano
stops.campa: D'Annunzio names Keller his Segretario d'Azione and sets him over the Ufficio Colpi di Mano — the Office of Bold Strokes. It is Keller who advises, spurs and goads the poet toward action; it is Keller who commands the men who will feed the blockaded city by piracy. He is, the Yoga journal will write of him, indescribably Italian, an irregular, a heretic, all will. D'Annunzio loves him as he wishes to be loved — the eccentric ace who gives everything away and keeps only the eagle and the sky.
stops.quote: È, in una parola, un italiano, indicibilmente italiano: è un irregolare, è un eretico, tutto volitivo.

segments.name: Gli Uscocchi — the pirate-raiders of the starving city, 1919–1920

stops.name: Lussinpiccolo — the capture of the Persia, thirteen thousand tons
stops.campa: On 10 October 1919, off the island of Lussinpiccolo, the Uscocchi take the steamship Persia — thirteen thousand tons of arms and supplies bound east for the anti-Bolshevik Russian armies. It is the founding coup of the Ufficio: the cargo is turned instead to Fiume, and the crew, moved or persuaded, largely joins the cause. The blockade meant to strangle the city now provisions it, and the pirate-republic proves it can feed and arm itself by the audacity of a wounded aviator and a handful of desperadoes.

stops.name: Fiume — the pig that broke through the fuselage
stops.campa: Not every raid is by sea. Keller descends upon a depot and carries off, among other spoils, a pig so vast that in flight it breaks clean through the floor of his fuselage — and he comes in to land with the beast's legs dangling as an original undercarriage. He flies with a fine porcelain tea-service and biscuits, and with abundant doses of cocaine. The Uscocco is a Sandokan of the Adriatic and a dandy at once: piracy performed as theatre, plunder as a work of art. Fiume laughs, and eats.
suggested_refs: Anecdote of the pig and the fuselage

stops.name: Fiume harbour — the seizure of the steamship Cogne
stops.campa: The blockade would starve Fiume; Keller's Uscocchi answer with piracy. Named for the Balkan corsairs of the sixteenth century, they board ships at sea and turn their holds toward the Quarnaro. In October 1920 seven of them, embarked in secret at Catania under Romano Manzutto, divert the great Ansaldo steamer Cogne — bound for Argentina with a cargo worth two hundred millions — into Keller's city. The poet's republic will eat because the ace's pirates have decreed that it shall. Supply, in Fiume, is a work of banditry raised to a fine art, and Keller is its impresario.

segments.name: Yoga — the union of free spirits, 1920

stops.name: Fiume — the tree-house, the eagle named Guido, the naked yogi
stops.campa: In Fiume Keller builds himself a small house in a tree and sleeps there, almost always half-naked, his trained Dinaric eagle — also named Guido — perched beside him. He walks the beach unclothed, exposes himself in gardens to scandalise the settled, keeps a blind Dalmatian ass and lives in what he calls the house of Diogenes. Hashish and cocaine, Vedanta and the sun: the ace has become a yogi-anarchist. D'Annunzio, delighted, once kidnaps the eagle as a prank — and must swiftly give it back.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Keller nude in Fiume

stops.name: Fiume — the founding of Yoga with Comisso
stops.campa: With the young writer Giovanni Comisso — his companion and lover, with whom he shares a hotel — Keller founds Yoga, an Union of Free Spirits tending toward perfection, and its journal of the same name. It is no party but a brotherhood of holy pranksters and eretici, esoteric and naturist, taking even the ancient swastika for a solar sign. Within the pirate-republic Keller makes a still wilder republic of the spirit: the freest cell of the freest city, where poetry, action and the East are declared the only politics worth the name.
stops.quote: Un'Unione di spiriti liberi tendenti alla perfezione.

segments.name: Il folle volo su Roma — the flight over Rome, November 1920

stops.name: Fiume airfield — the take-off in the SVA
stops.campa: Two days after Italy signs the Treaty of Rapallo — surrendering Fiume — Keller answers with the purest gesture the pirate-republic ever made. On 14 November 1920 he takes off in his Ansaldo SVA and points it at the capital, carrying red roses, a white rose, a bundle of carrots and turnips, and an enamelled chamber-pot. He will speak to Rome not in words but in objects: love to the people, contempt to the government. It is Fiume itself made flesh and set flying — a Dada raid before the word exists.

stops.name: The Vatican — the white rose for Frate Francesco
stops.campa: Over the Vatican Keller lets fall a single white rose — not for the Pope but for Frate Francesco, Brother Francis, the saint of the birds and of holy poverty. The gesture is entirely his: he salutes not the Church of power but the Franciscan spirit, the mendicant who owned nothing and loved everything. From the yogi-anarchist above St Peter's it is a benediction offered to the poorest, freest Christianity — one wanderer of the air blessing another who once walked barefoot through Umbria.
stops.quote_source: Guido Keller, dedication dropped over the Vatican, 14 November 1920

stops.name: The Quirinale — red roses for the Queen and the people of Italy
stops.campa: Over the Quirinal Keller drops seven red roses, dedicated to the Queen and to the people of Italy — a pledge of love to the nation, offered above the palace of its King. To the crown and the folk he brings flowers; the poison he reserves for the elected men who have signed away Fiume. In the theatre of his flight the roses are the whole of Italy that Keller still loves, kept carefully apart from the Parliament he is about to insult with all the splendour of his contempt.
stops.quote: Alla regina e al popolo d'Italia.
stops.quote_source: Guido Keller, dedication dropped over the Quirinale, 14 November 1920

stops.name: Montecitorio — the chamber-pot on the Parliament
stops.campa: Over the Palazzo di Montecitorio, seat of the Parliament, Keller drops an enamelled iron chamber-pot, hung with a bundle of yellow carrots and turnips and a message — the allegorical tangibility of their worth, handed to a government that governs by lies and by fear. The pitale misses the Chamber and lands on the roof of the Hotel Milan; no matter. The gesture is complete, indelible, pure Fiume: the pirate-republic of poets has answered the Treaty of Rapallo by defecating, symbolically and from the sky, upon the state.
stops.quote: Guido Keller, Ala Azione nello splendore, dona al Parlamento e al Governo che si reggono da tempo con la menzogna e con la paura, la tangibilità allegorica del Loro Valore. Roma, 14 del terzo mese della Reggenza.
stops.quote_source: Guido Keller, message attached to the chamber-pot dropped on Montecitorio, 14 November 1920
suggested_refs: The enamelled chamber-pot (pitale) of Guido Keller

stops.name: San Marino — the forced landing and the improvised embassy
stops.campa: Bad weather forces Keller down at the ancient free republic of San Marino, and the little state receives the aviator as a hero. Never at a loss, he improvises there a message from d'Annunzio to the Italian government and secures diplomatic credentials that let him slip back through the blockade to Fiume. The eagle of the Quarnaro, having dropped roses and merde upon Rome in a single morning, comes home protected by the papers of the oldest republic in the world. The whole flight has the logic of a dream, and the audacity of a myth.

segments.name: Natale di sangue e la fine — the fall of Fiume, 1920–1921

stops.name: Fiume — the Natale di sangue, the Christmas of Blood
stops.campa: At Christmas 1920 the Italian army, enforcing Rapallo, turns its guns on Fiume. The Natale di sangue — the Christmas of Blood — breaks the pirate-republic; a shell strikes the Governor's Palace itself and d'Annunzio yields to spare the city. Keller's dream ends where it lived, on the Quarnaro. Sixteen months of poetry and piracy, of eagles and chamber-pots and free unions of the spirit, close under artillery. The Comandante will withdraw to Lake Garda; his Segretario d'Azione will wander the earth, carrying Fiume with him like an incurable wound.

segments.name: Gli anni erranti — the wandering years, 1921–1929

stops.name: Rome — the March, and the fascism that distrusted him
stops.campa: Restless after Fiume, Keller joins the fascist movement and takes part in the March on Rome of October 1922 — yet the regime distrusts the heretic, and he it. He is too free, too mocking, too much the anarchist for the order the Blackshirts are building. The pirate of the Quarnaro cannot be domesticated into a functionary of the state he once dropped a chamber-pot upon. He is a man of one city and one dream, and that city has fallen; everything after is a search for something the century will not give him.

stops.name: Berlin — the aeronautical attaché
stops.campa: Keller returns to military flying and is sent to Berlin as aeronautical attaché to the Italian embassy. The ace who slept in a tree wears now the correct dress of a diplomat of the air. But the schemes and visions do not leave him: he dreams of aviation ventures, of new frontiers, of some impossible enterprise that might be Fiume again. The northern capital cannot hold the man of the Quarnaro any more than Milan could. He is always, everywhere, looking past the horizon for the republic that vanished.

stops.name: Benghazi — the desert flights over Libya
stops.campa: Keller flies over Libya, in the operations against the rebel tribes of Cyrenaica — the ace at war again, now above the desert instead of the Piave. But even the sands cannot fix him. The vision that drives him is not conquest but flight itself, the pure act, the splendour of action. He seeks in the empty sky what Fiume once gave him whole: a place where the free spirit might act without the ledger, the schoolmaster or the treaty. Libya is a station on a road that leads always outward, never home.

stops.name: The Amazon and Peru — up the great river, prospecting for gold
stops.campa: Keller crosses to South America and goes up the Amazon, visits Venezuela, and works in Peru as a prospector for gold. The Milanese aristocrat, the ace, the yogi, the pirate, is now a seeker in the green immensity — one of the atlas's wanderers who chase in far places the thing that eluded them at home. He finds no gold that holds. The eagle of Fiume has become a solitary figure on strange rivers, spending the last of a fortune and a legend on schemes that always dissolve into the next horizon.

stops.name: Ostia — the last poverty by the sea
stops.campa: Keller comes home poor, without prospects, and takes a room in a boarding house at Ostia, lodged for nothing by an old friend of the Fiume days. The aristocrat has given everything away, as was always his way; only the fellowship of a few aviators — de Bernardi among them — remains to him. By the sea at the mouth of the Tiber the eagle of the Quarnaro grows still. He is thirty-seven, and the century that could not use him has left him at last on the shore, waiting for the road.

stops.name: Magliano Sabina — the car crash on the rainy road
stops.campa: On the night of 9 November 1929, in the rain on a road near Magliano Sabina in the Sabine hills, Keller's Fiat 525 swerves and goes off a bridge. The war-hero Vittorio Montiglio dies beside him; Keller too is killed, thirty-seven years old. So ends the eagle of Fiume — not in the air he loved but on the earth, at the roadside, in a crash like the ones that take so many of the atlas's seekers. The wildest spirit of the pirate-republic of poets is stopped at last by a wet Sabine curve.

stops.name: Il Vittoriale — buried on the Colle delle Arche beside the Comandante
stops.campa: By d'Annunzio's own wish Keller is carried to the Vittoriale degli Italiani above Lake Garda and buried on the Colle delle Arche, among the legionaries of Fiume — the place where the Comandante himself will one day lie. The poet who loved him as he wished to be loved gives his Segretario d'Azione a tomb of honour on the sacred hill. So the eagle who slept in a tree comes to rest in stone beside his commander, and the pirate-republic of poets, dissolved on the Quarnaro, is reunited in the earth of Gardone.
stops.quote: Egli era stato uno dei pochissimi che hanno saputo amarmi come io voglio essere amato.
stops.quote_source: Gabriele d'Annunzio, on the death of Guido Keller, 1929
